titulo: Análise in silico do gene TP53 no câncer de pulmão: expressão gênica, prognóstico e potenciais interações moleculares
titulo_curto: The TP53 gene in lung cancer, investigated in public databases

estudo.situacao: Final report completed · not yet published

em_1_minuto.texto: Lung cancer is one of the deadliest cancers in the world, often because it is found at an advanced stage. The TP53 gene, the “guardian of the genome”, is frequently altered in these tumors.
Everything was done on the computer (in silico), with public data from patients with lung adenocarcinoma and six bioinformatics tools.
The tumor had more active TP53 than normal lung. In one analysis, people with more TP53 lived shorter; in another, there was no difference.

em_1_minuto.titulo: Leads to test in the lab
em_1_minuto.texto: TP53 sits at the center of a large protein network and is linked to 452 drugs and compounds. These are hypotheses that still need to be confirmed in experiments.

secoes.titulo: Why look at TP53 in lung cancer
secoes.lede: A common cancer that is often found late, and a gene that usually protects the body against tumors.

blocos.html:
Lung cancer is among the most common tumors and one of the leading causes of cancer death worldwide. In Brazil, INCA (the National Cancer Institute) estimated 32,560 cases per year between 2023 and 2025 (18,020 in men and 14,540 in women). Because it usually causes no symptoms early on, it is often found at an advanced stage: only 16% to 20% of people are alive 5 years after diagnosis.

The most common type is non-small cell lung cancer, which accounts for about 85% of cases. Within it, the most frequent subtype is adenocarcinoma, the focus of this study. Smoking is the main risk factor, but cases in people who have never smoked have been rising.

itens.texto: The gene that makes the p53 protein. It is a tumor suppressor: it helps control cell division, repair DNA and eliminate badly damaged cells.
A study done on the computer, with public data from thousands of patients. It is used to raise hypotheses that are later tested in the lab.

blocos.html: This study follows the same line as the study on the R337H variant: using bioinformatics to understand the role of TP53 in cancer.

secoes.lede: An exploratory study, done only with public data on lung adenocarcinoma.

itens.titulo: UALCAN · how much TP53 is in the tumor
itens.texto: Compared the gene's activity in 515 tumors and 59 normal lung samples from the TCGA project, and split the results by age and sex.

itens.titulo: KM Plotter · does TP53 change survival?
itens.texto: Split patients into two groups, with high and low TP53, and compared how long each group lived (Kaplan-Meier curves).

itens.titulo: UCSC Xena · checking in another database
itens.texto: Repeated the survival analysis with a different cutoff: 285 patients with high TP53 and 282 with low TP53.
Built the network of proteins that interact with p53.
Listed drugs and compounds with a described interaction with the gene. The original plan was to use CTD, which was unavailable in Brazil during the study.

itens.titulo: Metascape · which processes TP53 is involved in
itens.texto: Grouped TP53 and its linked genes by shared biological processes and signaling pathways.

blocos.html: Differences in gene activity were tested with each platform's statistical methods; survival, with the log-rank test and the hazard ratio (HR), with a 95% confidence interval.

secoes.lede: Choose a comparison to see the numbers.

parametros.leitura: In the 515 tumors, median TP53 activity was 52.2 TPM, versus 34.2 TPM in the 59 normal lung samples.
Men and women with the tumor had more active TP53 than normal lung; the median was slightly higher in women.
With high TP53, median survival was 62 months, versus 79.3 months with low TP53: a 29% higher risk of death (HR 1.29; 95% CI: 1.15 to 1.46; p = 0.000024).

blocos.nota: Medians reported in the final report. TPM = transcripts per million, a measure of how active the gene is.

blocos.alt: Box plot: the tumor box, in red, sits above the normal tissue box, in blue, with a table of values below
blocos.legenda: Figure 1 · TP53 activity in normal tissue (blue, 59 samples) and in lung adenocarcinoma (red, 515 samples), in transcripts per million (TPM). TCGA data.
blocos.credito: UALCAN, in Carvalho (2026), undergraduate research report

blocos.alt: Five colored boxes by age group, rising as age increases
blocos.legenda: Figure 2 · TP53 activity by age group. The median rises with age: 49.97 TPM from age 41 and 62.53 TPM between ages 81 and 100, versus 34.24 TPM in normal tissue.
blocos.credito: UALCAN, in Carvalho (2026), undergraduate research report

blocos.alt: Two step-shaped survival curves; the red one, high TP53, drops faster than the black one
blocos.legenda: Figure 3 · Survival in KM Plotter: patients with high TP53 (red) and low TP53 (black) over time in months. The more the curve drops, the more patients died.
blocos.credito: KM Plotter, in Carvalho (2026), undergraduate research report

blocos.html: The two survival analyses did not agree. In KM Plotter, high TP53 was linked to shorter survival. In UCSC Xena, with a different cutoff and a different group of patients, there was no difference between high and low TP53 (p = 0.89).

itens.texto: In STRING, p53 appeared at the center of a network with important regulatory proteins, such as ATM, SIRT1, MDM2, EP300 and CREBBP.
DGIdb listed 452 interactions between TP53 and drugs or compounds, but most still have no defined mechanism (whether they activate or inhibit).
Metascape linked the genes to processes of response to stimuli, cell cycle control, checkpoints and DNA damage response.

blocos.alt: Network of colored balls connected by lines, with TP53 in the center
blocos.legenda: Figure 4 · p53 interaction network in STRING. Each ball is a protein and each line a known or predicted interaction.
blocos.credito: STRING, in Carvalho (2026), undergraduate research report

blocos.alt: Network of colored dots in shades of purple, with the key to the cell cycle and DNA damage pathways
blocos.legenda: Figure 5 · Cell cycle and DNA damage response pathways in Metascape: cell cycle checkpoints, G1 to S transition, DNA damage response and the G2/M checkpoint.
blocos.credito: Metascape, in Carvalho (2026), undergraduate research report

secoes.titulo: What the results allow us to say, and what they don't yet
secoes.lede: Results that match the literature but are still hypotheses.

blocos.html:
The KM Plotter result agrees with the study by El-Arabey and colleagues (2023), in which high TP53 was also linked to a worse prognosis in lung adenocarcinoma. The UCSC Xena result agrees with Li and colleagues (2023): in TCGA data, TP53 activity alone did not change survival, but having a mutation in the gene did.

One explanation is that measuring the gene's activity does not tell whether the p53 protein works: in tumors, TP53 is often mutated. Differences between patient groups, the cutoffs used to separate “high” and “low”, and the statistical methods also play a role.

itens: This is an exploratory study done only with public data: the findings need to be validated in the lab.
Gene activity alone does not show whether the p53 protein is working.
The two survival tools used different groups and cutoffs and reached different results.
Most of the 452 drug interactions still have no known mechanism.

secoes.titulo: What the study shows so far
secoes.lede: A central gene in lung adenocarcinoma, with prognostic value that still needs to be confirmed.

blocos.html: TP53 is more active in lung adenocarcinoma than in normal lung, with a tendency to increase in older age groups and in both sexes. Its effect on survival varied with the tool used, as is also seen in the literature. The protein networks, pathways and drug interactions reinforce the role of TP53 in controlling the cell cycle and protecting DNA, and point to paths to test in the lab.

glossario.def: A study done on the computer, with databases and software, without lab experiments.
TP53 is the gene; p53 is the protein it makes, called the “guardian of the genome”.
A gene that helps stop cells from multiplying out of control.
The most common subtype of non-small cell lung cancer.
How active a gene is, that is, how many working copies (RNA) the cell makes of it.
Transcripts per million: a standardized measure of how active a gene is in a sample.
The Cancer Genome Atlas, a large public database with genetic data from thousands of tumors.
A step-shaped graph showing the percentage of patients alive over time.
Compares risk between two groups. HR 1.29 means 29% more risk in the high-TP53 group.
A map of which proteins bind to or work together inside the cell.
A control point where the cell checks that everything is fine before continuing to divide.
